title: Football Passing Drills for Beginners: Accuracy, Weight and Timing
summary: Try four simple football passing drills for beginners, with clear coaching points for accuracy, pass weight and choosing when to release the ball.
intro: A useful pass reaches a teammate in a way that helps her next action. Hitting a small target is a good start, but distance, timing and the receiver’s movement matter too. These STAR practices focus on delivering the ball; our separate first-touch guide covers what happens when it arrives. Use a safe, level space, a suitable ball and flat markers, and adjust distances to the player.

sections.title: Begin with a comfortable short pass
paragraphs: Stand a few metres apart. Approach the ball comfortably, place the supporting foot alongside it and use the inside of the other foot to guide it towards your partner. Keep the ankle steady through contact. Start slowly enough to notice the direction and pace rather than trying to strike hard.

Ask the receiver whether the pass was comfortable to control. If it repeatedly bounces, reduce the force and explore contact nearer the middle of the ball. If accuracy falls, shorten the distance. There is no need to demand identical body shapes from every player.

sections.title: Drill one: pass through a gate
paragraphs: Make a gate about a metre wide between two players. Pass along the ground through it, allowing a settling touch before returning. Begin with a generous target and gradually narrow it only if the task remains enjoyable.

Notice which side of the gate the ball misses. Change one detail, such as supporting-foot direction, then try again. Count a short run of comfortable passes if the player likes a challenge; a personal score is optional.

sections.title: Drill two: match the distance
paragraphs: Set one short and one longer passing distance. Alternate between them and ask the receiver to stay in place so the passer can judge how much force is needed. The longer pass should still be controllable.
Progress by letting the receiver choose either position before the pass. The passer now needs to look up and adjust, rather than repeat the same swing regardless of the situation.

sections.title: Drill three: pass into a moving path
paragraphs: A partner walks sideways across a wide gate. Play the ball into her path so she can collect it without stopping. Begin at walking pace, swap roles and then change direction.

A pass behind the runner often means the release was late or aimed at where she had been. Ask where she was going and try a slightly earlier release. Increase speed only when both players can work comfortably.

sections.title: Drill four: choose the open option
paragraphs: With three players, offer two receivers and let a passive defender block one passing lane. The passer can use the free receiver or wait while the angle changes. Rotate roles regularly.
This is where passing practice becomes a football decision. Praise recognising a blocked lane and finding another solution, rather than treating every retained ball as a missed opportunity to pass.

sections.title: Common questions about passing practice
paragraphs: Should every pass be first time? No. A settling touch can help a beginner find balance; first-time play is useful when the situation allows it. Should she always pass forwards? No. A sideways or backwards pass may keep possession and create a better next attack.

Can she practise alone? A safe rebound wall can work where permission and surroundings allow it. Mark a broad target, stand close enough to control the return and avoid windows, people and roads. Partner practice adds information that a wall cannot provide.

practice: Choose two drills for a short practice, with breaks. Finish by asking which pass helped the receiver most. Next time, change the receiver’s position rather than simply making every pass longer.
takeaways: Judge a pass by how it helps the receiver.
Adjust pace to distance and movement.
Add a choice once the basic action feels comfortable.

title: Ball Mastery Drills for Kids: Five Ways to Build Close Control
summary: Five ball mastery drills for children, using one ball and a small space, with easier options and ways to connect close control to football decisions.
intro: Ball mastery means becoming comfortable moving the ball with different parts of the feet. It can help a child explore touches without waiting in a queue or worrying about an opponent. It is one part of learning football: being quick at a footwork pattern does not automatically mean knowing when to pass or dribble. These five STAR activities start with control and finish with a choice.

sections.title: Set up a space she can manage
paragraphs: Use a clear area with a level, non-slip surface and room to move away from the ball. Flat markers or safe landmarks are enough. Leave space between players and keep away from furniture, roads and fragile objects.

Start without a timer. A younger beginner might explore one action for a few attempts; an experienced player might combine movements. Let coordination and interest determine the challenge rather than age alone.

sections.title: One: gentle sole rolls
paragraphs: Rest the sole lightly on the ball, roll it across the body and stop it with the other foot. Keep the standing knee comfortable and the movement small. If balancing is difficult, roll and stop with the same foot before changing sides.
Add an exit: after two or three rolls, move the ball towards a marker and walk after it. The final touch should leave the ball reachable, not trapped beneath the body.

sections.title: Two: inside-to-inside touches
paragraphs: Use the insides of the feet to move the ball gently from side to side. Begin with a pause between contacts. Explore how little force is needed to keep it nearby.
Then travel forwards a few steps. If the pattern becomes hurried, return to slower touches. The aim is comfortable control, not a race against a video or another player.

sections.title: Three: inside and outside on one foot
paragraphs: Use the inside of one foot to guide the ball across, then its outside to move it back. Work over a small distance and swap feet. Allow extra touches whenever needed.
Place a wide gate ahead. After the pattern, choose either side and carry the ball through. This links manipulation to moving somewhere useful rather than keeping the ball permanently under the feet.

sections.title: Four: stop, look and go
paragraphs: Carry the ball slowly around the area. A partner points towards an available gate. Stop the ball if needed, look and move towards it. Use a spoken or visual signal that suits the player.
Avoid requiring a child to stare upwards continuously. Brief glances between touches are more realistic. Change the signal slowly enough to allow processing and safe movement.

sections.title: Five: protect an exit
paragraphs: Make two gates. A partner stands well back and gradually closes one route without tackling. The player uses touches to move towards the other exit. Swap roles and let her explain what she noticed.
This activity adds a reason to control the ball. If both exits feel blocked, widen the area or slow the partner down. More complicated footwork is not always the best answer.

sections.title: How to notice progress
paragraphs: Look for a ball that stays within reach, smoother changes of direction and a player willing to try both feet. Ask which movement felt useful. A short, happy practice is more valuable than continuing after frustration has taken over.
Keep games and team football in the picture. Ball mastery can prepare touches, but teammates and opponents provide the changing information that makes those touches meaningful.

practice: Let the player choose two movements and invent a route between three safe markers. Ask her to show a slow version, then change the route. Finish with an open-gate choice rather than a speed test.
takeaways: Start with control and balance.
Let both feet explore without demanding equal speed.
Connect footwork to an exit, opponent or next action.

title: How to Shield the Ball in Football Without Pushing or Holding
summary: Learn how to shield the ball in football using body position, reachable touches and an exit, with a gentle partner practice for young players.
intro: Shielding gives a player time when an opponent is close and a forward route is blocked. She places her body between the opponent and the ball while keeping it within playing distance. The purpose is to retain options until she can pass, turn or move away. It should never become an exercise in tolerating heavy contact or proving who is strongest.

sections.title: Find the opponent before choosing the touch
paragraphs: A glance before receiving can reveal where pressure is coming from. If the opponent approaches from the left, an appropriate touch towards the right may help keep the ball farther away. The best solution may also be a quick pass before pressure arrives.

Begin with a partner approaching slowly from a known direction. Let the player get used to recognising the pressure before adding uncertainty. If she cannot locate the opponent, make the approach clearer and give her more time.

sections.title: Use a balanced position
paragraphs: Turn slightly sideways so the body separates opponent and ball. Keep the knees comfortable and the feet ready to adjust. A wide, rigid stance can make the next movement harder; balance should allow a step, pivot or pass.
Use the foot farther from the opponent when it helps. Keep the ball close enough to play. If a touch sends it several strides away, the body can no longer protect it effectively.

sections.title: Protect space without committing a foul
paragraphs: Keep arms in a natural position for balance. Do not grab a shirt, lock an arm around an opponent or extend an arm to push her away. Do not step across a player’s path merely to block her when the ball is beyond playing distance.

A coach should explain and supervise any contact. Start with shadowing and no tackles. Stop if either player feels uncomfortable; introduce realistic pressure gradually with suitable partners and clear boundaries.

sections.title: Move the ball as the picture changes
paragraphs: Shielding is rarely a frozen pose. Small touches can keep the ball on the safer side as the defender moves. If pressure switches sides, the player may need to pivot, change feet or release a pass.
Ask what the defender has left available. A player who protects the ball successfully and then passes backwards has kept the attack alive. Turning towards goal is one option, not a compulsory ending.

sections.title: A gentle two-gate shielding practice
paragraphs: Make a comfortable playing area with two exit gates. One player starts with the ball, while a partner shadows from behind and to one side without contact. The ball carrier keeps it reachable, then chooses a gate when space appears.

Progress to light, agreed attempts to intercept the ball rather than pushing the player. Add a supporting teammate so a pass can also count as an escape. Keep rounds brief, swap roles and pause to discuss the choices.

sections.title: When shielding does not help
paragraphs: Near your own goal, holding the ball under pressure can create unnecessary danger. Follow the team’s instructions and use an available safe pass. Likewise, a clear forward route may be better used immediately than delayed by turning back into pressure.

If she loses possession, review the moment before contact. Was the touch too far away? Was support missing? Did she see the opponent? Those questions give her something to change without blaming her size or bravery.

practice: Try shadow shielding with two exits and no tackling. Ask the player to name an available route before she uses it. Add a support pass when she is ready, keeping the emphasis on escaping pressure safely.
takeaways: Keep the ball within reach and away from pressure.
Use balance and movement rather than pushing or holding.
Finish with an available pass, turn or carry.

title: Football Turns Explained: Drag Back, Inside Hook and Cruyff Turn
summary: Learn three football turns step by step, then practise choosing a drag back, inside hook or Cruyff turn when the space ahead closes.
intro: A turn changes the direction of play when the route ahead is blocked or a better option appears elsewhere. Players do not need a collection of elaborate tricks to begin. A few comfortable actions, used after checking the space, can be enough. This guide focuses on reversing or changing direction; beating an opponent while moving forwards is covered in our separate dribbling guide.

sections.title: Check where the turn will take you
paragraphs: Before turning, notice the space behind and beside you. A technically tidy move can still take the ball towards another opponent. Begin with a clear exit and explore the action slowly, then introduce a partner who closes one route.

Set two gates a few steps apart in a safe area. Carry the ball towards a marker, turn and leave through a gate. The marker is a location cue, not a defender: later, use an opponent so the player learns when the move helps.

sections.title: How to do a drag back
paragraphs: Place the sole lightly on the ball and draw it backwards while turning the body towards the intended exit. Take the next touch into the new direction. Start from stillness before trying it while moving.

If the ball gets trapped underneath, make the pull slightly clearer and give the standing foot room to turn. Avoid leaning back or trying to rotate quickly on a planted foot. Keep movements comfortable and stop if something hurts.

sections.title: How to do an inside hook
paragraphs: Move towards the ball, bring the inside of the foot around its far side and guide it back across the body into a new direction. Turn with it and take a controlled next touch.
A common difficulty is hooking the ball behind the standing leg so it becomes hard to reach. Start with a small change of direction, then explore a larger turn once the player can leave smoothly.

sections.title: How to do a Cruyff turn
paragraphs: Shape as though you may pass or cross. Use the inside of that foot to guide the ball behind the supporting leg, then turn and follow it into the new space. Begin at walking pace without an opponent.

The disguise matters only if there is a believable passing or crossing option. Do not demand a large swing or dramatic body movement. A small, balanced action can be easier to control and recover from.

sections.title: Add an opponent and a reason
paragraphs: Ask a partner to approach slowly towards one gate. The player can continue if it remains open or turn towards the other gate. Initially, the partner shadows without tackling. Later, allow a controlled attempt to win the ball.

Do not tell the player which turn to use on every attempt. Ask what she saw and whether the ball stayed reachable. She may discover that a simple inside hook works better than a Cruyff turn in a particular space.

sections.title: Questions players often ask
paragraphs: Which turn is best? The one that suits the pressure, available space and next action. Must she use both feet? Explore both, but allow different rates of progress. Does a turn need to look fast? A slower turn that retains possession may be useful.

How does it reach matches? Choose a recognisable moment, such as a blocked forward route near the touchline, and look for an opportunity in club training. There is no need to force the turn when a simple pass is already available.

practice: Explore each turn without pressure, then let a partner close one of two exits. Choose the action that preserves the available route. Finish by describing when a turn helped and when continuing forwards was easier.
takeaways: Check the exit before turning.
Learn slowly enough to keep balance.
Choose the turn for the situation, not its name.

title: The Offside Rule Explained Simply for Players and Parents
summary: Understand the offside rule through simple football examples: position, involvement, pass timing and why throw-ins, goal kicks and corners are different.
intro: Offside is easier to learn when you separate two questions: where was the attacker when a teammate played the ball, and did she then become involved? This is an introduction to the standard law, with original STAR examples. Youth formats can have different arrangements, so check the competition rules before applying it to a particular age group.

sections.title: Position alone is not an offence
paragraphs: In the standard law, an attacker is in an offside position if a playable part of her head, body or feet is in the opponents’ half and nearer their goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent. Hands and arms do not count. Being level is onside.
Position alone does not mean a whistle. The attacker must become involved, for example by playing the ball or interfering with an opponent. It is not always enough to say that she did not touch it.

sections.title: Freeze the picture when the pass is played
paragraphs: Example: a midfielder prepares a through pass. The striker starts level with the second-last opponent, then accelerates beyond her after the ball is played. Receiving it behind the defence does not make that run offside.

Now reverse the timing. The striker starts beyond the offside line before the pass is played and comes back to collect it. Returning towards the ball does not erase her earlier position if she becomes involved in that phase.

sections.title: Why counting defenders can be misleading
paragraphs: The law refers to opponents, including the goalkeeper, rather than requiring a particular number of outfield defenders. A keeper may have moved upfield. Remember the ball’s position too: an attacker level with or behind it is not in an offside position.

For a simple practice, use markers for the goalkeeper and another opponent. Move the goalkeeper away and ask which opponent now determines the line. Keep the task about reading the arrangement rather than memorising shirt numbers.

sections.title: Three direct-receipt exceptions
paragraphs: There is no offside offence when receiving directly from a throw-in, goal kick or corner kick. A later teammate’s touch creates a new moment to assess. Free kicks do not share this exemption.
Example: a player receives a throw-in beyond the defenders and passes to a teammate. Judge that teammate’s position at the new pass; the whole attack is not permanently exempt.

sections.title: Deflections and involvement need care
paragraphs: A rebound or deflection does not automatically reset offside. An opponent’s deliberate play is treated differently, with deliberate saves an exception. These judgements have detailed conditions in IFAB Law 11.

For players, the useful habit is to keep playing until the whistle and leave the decision to the officials. From the sideline, avoid teaching that any defender’s touch makes a player onside. A short introductory guide cannot cover every unusual incident.

sections.title: Practise the timing without an argument
paragraphs: Use a passer, runner and a marked defensive line. Begin with walking movements and pause as the passer contacts the ball. Ask the runner to check her starting position, then try a curved or delayed run.
Progress to a defender who can move. The runner needs to watch both the passer and the line. Celebrate good timing even if the eventual pass is inaccurate; the two actions can be reviewed separately.

sections.title: Common questions
paragraphs: Can she be offside in her own half? Not under the standard position definition. Does running past the defender always mean offside? No: timing and the ball’s position matter. Does being far from the ball guarantee she cannot offend? No: involvement can include interference.

Does every children’s match use offside? Check the actual format and league. Teach the rule that applies to her match and introduce the wider law gradually, without making a beginner afraid to run forwards.

practice: Lay out a small pitch using counters or cones. Create three moments: a well-timed run, an early run and direct receipt from a throw-in. Ask the player to explain which moment matters before moving into a gentle passing practice.
takeaways: Judge position when a teammate plays the ball.
An offside position and an offside offence are different.
Check youth competition rules and respect the officials.

title: How to Take a Throw-In: Football Rules, Technique and Practice
summary: Learn the basic throw-in rules and a simple technique, then practise finding a teammate and retaining possession after the restart.
intro: A throw-in is a chance to restart possession together. Sending it the farthest is not always useful: the receiver needs space, support and a ball she can control. This guide explains standard throw-in basics and gives a STAR partner activity. Some youth formats use alternative restarts, so check what applies to the player’s competition.

sections.title: The basic throw-in rules
paragraphs: When the whole ball crosses a touchline, the throw-in normally goes to the opponents of the player who last touched it. At delivery, face the field, use both hands and bring the ball from behind and over the head. Part of each foot must be on the touchline or on the ground outside it.

Take the throw from where the ball left the field. Opponents must stay at least two metres from that point. The thrower cannot touch the ball again until another player has touched it, and a goal cannot be scored directly from the throw.

sections.title: Start with a balanced standing throw
paragraphs: Hold the ball comfortably in both hands. Try a staggered stance and bring it behind the head before releasing forwards over the head. Keep part of each foot grounded at release. Start with a short distance and a relaxed movement.

If one foot repeatedly lifts, slow down and shorten the target distance. Practise the action without a run-up. The goal is a repeatable legal restart, not an adult-style long throw. Do not force a movement that causes back or shoulder discomfort.

sections.title: Choose the receiver before choosing the distance
paragraphs: Look for an unmarked teammate or a teammate moving towards an available space. A short throw can be effective if she has a return option. A longer throw into a crowded area may simply hand possession away.

Ask the receiver whether the delivery helped. Could she meet it comfortably? Did it force her towards the touchline? Change the target or release, rather than assuming every lost ball means the throw needed more power.

sections.title: Receivers can help the thrower
paragraphs: Standing still directly behind a defender gives the thrower little to work with. Make a small movement away and then towards an open angle, or offer a different distance from a teammate.

Agree a clear signal and avoid several players running into the same space. The nearest player may offer short while another becomes a supporting option. Follow the club coach’s restart arrangements rather than introducing a competing team routine.

sections.title: Move again after the release
paragraphs: Once the throw has reached another player, the thrower can become a return option. Step onto the pitch and find a helpful angle, while staying aware of opponents and the touchline.
Try a simple three-player sequence: throw to a receiver, return the ball with the feet, then pass to a third player. Begin without opposition. Later, allow a defender to choose which option to cover.

sections.title: Common questions and mistakes
paragraphs: Can a player be offside directly from a throw-in? No, although a subsequent teammate’s pass is assessed normally. Must the whole foot stay behind the line? No: the standard law allows part of each foot on the line or grounded outside it.

Why does a throw feel difficult in matches? Often the thrower has no clear option. Practise the receiver’s movement and support as well as the throwing action. Check local restart rules, and follow the referee’s instructions on the day.

practice: Set two receiving gates a comfortable distance away. A partner moves towards one and calls or signals. Deliver a balanced throw, then step in to offer a return pass after her touch. Swap roles and review which delivery was easiest to use.
takeaways: Learn the legal action before adding distance.
Give the thrower a clear receiving option.
Support the next pass after the throw.

title: How to Take a Corner Kick: Delivery, Short Corners and Practice
summary: Improve corner-kick delivery with target zones, short-corner options and simple practice that suits a young player’s range and team instructions.
intro: A good corner creates a playable opportunity for the team. It does not have to travel across the entire penalty area or imitate a professional player’s delivery. Young players can work on a comfortable striking action, a sensible target and a shared plan. These are STAR practice suggestions; agree match routines with the club coach.

sections.title: Know the restart before practising the kick
paragraphs: Under the standard law, the ball is stationary in the corner area nearest where it crossed the goal line. The flag stays in place. It is in play when kicked and clearly moving; the taker cannot touch it again before another player does.

Opponents remain at least 9.15 metres from the corner arc until it is in play under the standard law. A goal can be scored directly against the opponents. Youth formats may use modified arrangements: check the actual competition.

sections.title: Pick a target within comfortable range
paragraphs: Mark a generous landing or receiving zone, initially quite close. Start with a delivery the player can control. If she strains to reach a distant target, move it nearer and explore a short-corner option.

Choose the target with teammates in mind. A delivery that repeatedly clears everyone may look powerful while offering little. The useful question is whether someone can reach it and continue the attack.

sections.title: Build the contact before adding curl
paragraphs: Use a comfortable approach and a balanced supporting foot. Explore how contact changes the ball’s path. Begin with a simple pass or low delivery, then work on a lifted ball only when the player is ready.

An inswinger curves towards goal and an outswinger curves away. Both can be useful, but curl is not compulsory. Trying to create dramatic movement before controlling the basic strike can make accuracy harder. Work with a coach to find an action that suits her.

sections.title: Treat the short corner as a real option
paragraphs: A teammate can offer a short pass, then help change the angle for another delivery or keep possession. She needs an available route and awareness of the nearest opponent, rather than waiting beside the taker without a plan.

There is no offside offence from receiving directly from the corner. After a teammate plays the ball again, assess the next phase normally. Players should understand this before relying on a return pass.

sections.title: Practise the delivery and the next ball
paragraphs: Use two target zones and a receiver. Start with low passes into space, then vary which zone the receiver approaches. The receiver can control and pass into a small target rather than heading or shooting through a crowd.

Add a defender gradually to make the choice matter. Keep people clear of repeated strikes and retrieve balls only when the area is safe. This activity does not require heading; follow current FA age and competition guidance if aerial work is planned.

sections.title: Remember what happens if possession is lost
paragraphs: The corner taker and supporting players should know their team’s recovery jobs. Not everyone needs to run into the penalty area. Someone may need to offer a safe pass or help protect against a counterattack.

If a corner fails, identify the cause. Was the delivery out of range, the target occupied, the timing wrong or the receiver unsupported? Change one part at a time. Repeatedly demanding more power rarely answers all those questions.

practice: Mark a nearby short-pass gate and a wider receiving zone. Let a partner show which is available before the kick. Play to the useful option, then include one further pass. Judge controllable deliveries rather than distance alone.
takeaways: Choose a target the player can reach comfortably.
Practise short corners as well as direct deliveries.
Plan support and recovery with the club coach.

title: How to Play Full-Back in Football: Defending, Support and Overlaps
summary: A practical full-back guide covering positioning, defending wide areas, supporting a winger, overlapping runs and recovering when possession changes.
intro: A full-back helps protect the wide area and connects defence with the players ahead. The role changes with formation, age and the coach’s instructions: some full-backs stay deeper, while others are asked to attack frequently. Start by understanding the team’s plan. This guide focuses on those wide defensive and supporting decisions rather than repeating the general positions guide.

sections.title: Find your place in the defensive unit
paragraphs: Notice the ball, your nearest centre-back and any opponent who could receive behind you. When play is on the opposite side, you may need to move infield to help protect central space. When it comes towards your side, prepare to move out together.

Ask the coach how close she wants you to stay to the centre-back and who covers when you press. There is no single correct position for every full-back. The space behind you matters as much as the opponent directly ahead.

sections.title: Approach the winger with control
paragraphs: Move towards the receiver while the ball travels, then slow enough to react. Avoid arriving so quickly that one touch takes the attacker past. A balanced position lets you retreat, delay or challenge when the opportunity appears.

The team may ask you to show the attacker towards the touchline or towards covering support. Follow that instruction rather than automatically forcing every opponent the same way. Staying patient can give teammates time to recover.

sections.title: Offer a useful passing angle
paragraphs: When your team has the ball, move where the passer can see you without sending you straight into pressure. A position slightly wider or deeper may open a safer lane than standing flat alongside an opponent.

Before receiving, check the winger ahead and the support inside. If the forward pass is blocked, retaining possession through the centre-back or goalkeeper can help the team move the opposition. Your role is not measured only by forward passes.

sections.title: Overlap when there is room and cover
paragraphs: An overlap is a run outside the teammate carrying the ball. It can offer a pass or draw an opponent away. Time it so the teammate has a chance to recognise the option rather than arriving early and standing beyond her.

Check who protects the space you leave. If a teammate is already making an attacking run, staying behind the ball might help more. An underlap goes inside the wide teammate; use it when it fits the coach’s plan and the space is available.

sections.title: Recover when the attack breaks down
paragraphs: As possession changes, identify the immediate danger. Sometimes you can pressure the ball; sometimes protecting the route towards goal is more urgent. Communicate with the centre-back and winger rather than chasing the nearest opponent automatically.
On recovery, keep checking runners as well as the ball. Getting back quickly helps, but returning to a useful position matters more than a sprint that leaves a central attacker free.

sections.title: A full-back and winger practice
paragraphs: In a safe wide channel, use a full-back, winger and one passive defender. The full-back passes forward and chooses whether to support underneath or overlap. The winger can return the ball or continue into space.

Add an opponent only when the movement is clear, then include a recovery gate towards the defending end. On a turnover, both attackers recover to protect it. Swap roles so the player experiences what her teammate needs.

sections.title: Common questions
paragraphs: Does a full-back have to be fast? Speed can help, but positioning, timing and communication also matter. Must she always overlap? No: the team needs balance. What should a young full-back work on first? Pick one recurring situation with her coach, such as receiving under pressure or delaying a winger.
If she also plays other positions, keep those opportunities. Learning what a winger sees can improve her decisions at full-back without fixing her to one role too early.

practice: Choose one wide situation from a match. Recreate it slowly with a winger and a passive defender, comparing a supporting angle with an overlap. Ask what changed for the player on the ball.
takeaways: Defend as part of a unit.
Support the winger before deciding to run beyond her.
Check cover and recovery when attacking.

title: How to Play Striker in Football: Movement, Link Play and Box Runs
summary: Learn how a striker creates passing options, times runs behind defenders, links play and moves in the box, with an adaptable practice for young forwards.
intro: Playing striker involves much more than shooting. A forward can help the team by creating space, connecting passes and occupying defenders, even in a match without a goal. This guide looks at the decisions before the finish. Our separate shooting-accuracy article covers striking practice, while this one explains how to arrive in a position where a finish becomes possible.

sections.title: Decide whether to come short or run behind
paragraphs: Look at the passer first. If she is under pressure and looking for support, showing to feet may help. If she has time and space to pass forwards, a run behind a defender may become useful.

Vary your movement rather than making the same run every time. A short movement towards the ball can draw a defender out; a later run into the space behind may create a different option. The passer still decides whether the ball can reach you.

sections.title: Time the run with the ball carrier
paragraphs: Starting early can leave you waiting beyond the defence or in an offside position. Watch for the passer preparing to release the ball and check the defensive line. A curved run can help you remain available while changing direction.

Practise with a passer and a moving defender rather than only a stationary cone. Ask whether the pass and run met at the same moment. A good run may still go unused, so do not judge every attempt by receiving the ball.

sections.title: Link play with a simple next action
paragraphs: When receiving with your back towards goal, check whether you can turn safely. If pressure is close, a short lay-off to a supporting teammate may help more than trying to spin through a defender.

Move again after the lay-off. You might create a return passing lane, pull the defender away or become available nearer the box. Keep the first practice gentle so the receiver can learn the pattern before coping with contact.

sections.title: Find space in the penalty area
paragraphs: Standing beside a defender makes a pass easier to track. A small movement away, followed by a change towards an available lane, can make the defender adjust. Watch the player delivering the ball and arrive where the pass can actually travel.

Near-post, far-post and cut-back spaces are possibilities rather than compulsory destinations. Coordinate with teammates so everyone does not attack the same lane. A ground-pass finishing activity can teach this timing without aerial challenges.

sections.title: Help when your team does not have the ball
paragraphs: Ask the coach where pressing should begin and which passing route she wants you to discourage. Running directly at every defender may use energy while leaving an easy pass open.

A curved approach can put pressure on the ball while reducing one option, but the rest of the team needs to act together. If teammates are not ready, holding position and screening a pass may fit the plan better.

sections.title: A three-player striker practice
paragraphs: Use a passer, striker and supporting player, with a broad target gate beyond them. The striker can come short, lay off and move again, or run towards the gate for a through pass. Begin without a defender.

Add a shadow defender who chooses to follow closely or leave space. The striker and passer now choose together. Rotate roles, keep distances comfortable and discuss the information behind the action rather than insisting on one rehearsed sequence.

sections.title: What if the goals are not coming?
paragraphs: Review useful actions: creating a passing option, keeping possession, making a well-timed run or helping the team defend. Goals depend partly on service and match situations, so a scoreless game does not explain the whole performance.

Choose a specific next step with the player. For example, work on checking the passer before a run, rather than setting a goal quota that she cannot fully control. Keep ambition connected to actions she can practise.

practice: Try the come-short or run-behind activity with a partner showing different passing pictures. Pause before the pass and explain the choice. Later, add a defender and let the decision happen naturally.
takeaways: Read the passer before committing to a run.
Link play and move again.
Judge contributions as well as goals.

title: Is One-to-One Football Coaching Worth It for Your Daughter?
summary: Decide whether private football coaching suits your daughter, with questions about goals, coaching quality, cost, progress and its place alongside club football.
intro: One-to-one football coaching can be worthwhile when a player wants focused help and the sessions address a clear need. It is an optional addition to football, not a requirement for progress or a promise of academy selection. For a family deciding whether to spend money, the useful question is what the coaching would add to the football she already has.

sections.title: Start with a specific reason
paragraphs: Ask the player what she wants help with. She might feel rushed when receiving, want to use her other foot or need a calmer setting to explore a skill. A specific example gives a coach something to assess and a family something to review.

Avoid booking purely because other players have extra sessions. If she is happy, learning and getting opportunities at her club, more coaching may not be a priority. Her willingness matters as much as the adult’s ambition.

sections.title: What individual coaching can add
paragraphs: A coach can adjust the pace, explanation and challenge around one player. There is time to repeat an action, ask questions and change the task when something is unclear. Some players value that uninterrupted attention.

The session should still connect to football decisions. For example, after practising a turn, a coach can vary the pressure or available exit. Repeating a movement neatly is useful preparation, but the player also needs to recognise when it helps.

sections.title: What it cannot replace
paragraphs: Team football provides teammates, opponents, shared decisions and match experiences that a single coach cannot fully reproduce. Individual coaching should support that environment and respect the club coach’s team instructions.

It cannot guarantee trials, scholarships, selection or a professional future. Be cautious of promises based on paying for a programme. A responsible discussion explains the work and its limits, leaving room for changing goals.

sections.title: Questions to ask before paying
paragraphs: Ask who will coach, what relevant qualifications and safeguarding arrangements apply, whether parents can observe and how the venue is confirmed. Discuss any support needs privately and ask how the session would be adapted.

Ask about the full cost, session length, cancellations, travel, equipment and any longer commitment. Current terms matter more than a headline price. A family should understand what is included before deciding whether it fits their budget.

sections.title: Agree how progress will be reviewed
paragraphs: Choose an observable focus, such as receiving away from nearby pressure and identifying an available pass. Ask the player what feels clearer and invite the coach to explain examples of change.

Some improvement appears in practice before it becomes reliable in matches. Review whether the sessions remain useful and enjoyable, without treating slow transfer as a failure. You should also be able to pause or change direction when circumstances change.

sections.title: When another option may suit better
paragraphs: A small group may offer more interaction and different opponents. Club training may already provide the right challenge. Informal play or a simple home activity may be enough for the current goal.

If the player is tired, overwhelmed or losing enjoyment, adding a session may make the week harder. First discuss what she wants to keep, reduce or change. Extra coaching should have a place in her life rather than take over it.

sections.title: Exploring individual coaching at STAR
paragraphs: STAR provides independent girls’ football development in Somerset, including Taunton, Bridgwater and Wellington. Individual options vary by age and programme; compare the current programme information before choosing.

The free 30-minute assessment and introduction provides a starting conversation about her experience, needs and possible next steps. It carries no commitment to join. STAR confirms the date and venue separately; submitting a request does not reserve a paid programme place.

practice: Together, write one football situation she would like help with, one question for a coach and a budget you can comfortably manage. Compare the answers after an introductory conversation before committing to regular sessions.
takeaways: Begin with her reason for wanting help.
Ask about quality, safeguarding, full cost and review.
Keep individual work connected to club football and enjoyment.

title: How Our Prestige Programme Aligns with Elite Pathways Like INAC Kobe Leonessa
summary: How INAC Kobe Leonessa’s academy principles resonate with STAR’s individual, long-term Prestige Programme, with practical football ideas to try.
intro: At STAR we look at how leading clubs and academies develop young players. INAC Kobe Leonessa’s academy describes a pathway through age-group teams and an approach that considers the player’s development as a person. Several of its principles resonate with the way we work in our Prestige Programme. STAR is independent and has no stated partnership with INAC Kobe Leonessa.

sections.title: Age-appropriate development over forced progress
paragraphs: INAC’s academy describes consistent, age-appropriate development as players progress towards the senior game. The Prestige Programme follows a long-term approach for girls aged 11–18: we identify priorities for each player’s current stage rather than expecting everyone to follow the same timetable.
For one player that might mean building confidence receiving the ball; for another, recognising passing options under pressure or refining a turn. We discuss progress against her own starting point.

sections.title: Individual attention alongside a clear pathway
paragraphs: INAC has football school and youth teams at different stages, with a pathway towards its senior team. STAR’s Prestige Programme has a different role: it provides individual coaching alongside a girl’s existing club football.
We work on specific technical needs and confidence, then help her consider how to use that learning in her team’s training and matches. Progress takes time and looks different for every player.

sections.title: Developing the person as well as the player
paragraphs: INAC’s academy philosophy includes manners, cooperation and independence alongside football development. At STAR we also value the person behind the player.

We listen to how she responds to challenge, communicates and feels about setbacks. Confidence can change during the teenage years, so we adjust our approach to the individual rather than assuming every girl experiences the same difficulties.

sections.title: Quality of practice
paragraphs: At STAR we put these broad development principles into practice by choosing a clear technical focus and giving the player time to explore it. A session might centre on receiving under pressure, changing direction or recognising options in tight spaces.

We use purposeful repetition, specific feedback and gradual changes in challenge. A player can then try the action in a more game-like situation and discuss what helped. These are STAR’s coaching choices, not a claim that INAC uses the same individual drills.

sections.title: Supporting ambition and enjoyment
paragraphs: The Prestige Programme is for girls who want to develop their game, while recognising that their goals and circumstances can change. We listen to the player and aim to make sessions purposeful and supportive.
A player should leave with a clearer idea of what she worked on and an opportunity to try it again, without feeling that every mistake defines her.

sections.title: What this means in practice
paragraphs: A Prestige player receives coaching matched to her current level, clear technical priorities, individual attention and a long-term view. The work supports her existing team football and is shaped around her needs and goals.
INAC’s environment and STAR’s are different. Our comparison is about principles that influence our thinking; it does not suggest an affiliation or a route into INAC.

sections.title: Applying the ideas to football
paragraphs: These are practical STAR examples inspired by the broad principles of patient technical development and decision-making. They are not presented as INAC academy drills. Choose one focus with the player and adapt the space, pace and repetitions to her age, confidence and available energy.

Look before receiving: with a partner, ask the player to glance over her shoulder before a gentle pass arrives. The partner can indicate a colour or point to a side; the player checks and tells them what she saw. Begin without pressure and give her time.

First touch towards space: place two small cone gates a few steps apart. Receive a pass with a comfortable, open body position and guide the first touch towards a chosen gate. Try both feet, then vary which gate is open before the ball arrives.

Pass and find a new angle: pass to a partner, move to a different position and offer for the return. Notice how a small movement creates a clearer passing line. Start slowly, then add a passive defender or a time constraint if appropriate.

Make a choice in a one-versus-one: set up two gates and let the player decide whether to change direction or protect the ball as a partner applies gentle pressure. Ask what she noticed; gradually adjust space or pressure rather than demanding a particular move every time.
Keep practice short and enjoyable, pause when needed, and try one idea in club training when the opportunity fits. Ask the player what she would like to practise again.

sections.title: Experience the approach
paragraphs: If you would like to explore whether the Prestige Programme would suit your daughter, we offer a free 30-minute assessment with no commitment. She can experience the coaching and you can discuss how we would support her development. The venue will be confirmed when arranging the assessment.

practice: Choose one idea from the football tips above and agree a comfortable next step with the player. To experience the Prestige approach, arrange a free 30-minute assessment; the venue will be confirmed when booking.
takeaways: Match the challenge to the player and her stage of development.
Give technical actions time to develop, then explore them in game-like situations.
Support ambition, enjoyment and existing club football.

title: Building confidence, one football moment at a time
summary: Help a player take the next small step without making confidence another test.
intro: Confidence can look different from one session to the next. A player may happily try a new turn in practice but hesitate when a defender closes her down in a match. That does not mean the practice was wasted. The situation has changed: there is less time, more uncertainty and often a stronger feeling of being watched. Start by finding out which part feels difficult, then make the next step clear enough to attempt.

sections.title: Find the situation behind the feeling
paragraphs: “Be more confident” is difficult to act on. Ask where the hesitation happens. Is it receiving with someone behind her, making a mistake in front of teammates, or asking the coach a question? Listen without immediately explaining why she should not worry. Her answer gives you something specific to work with. A player who fears losing possession needs a different conversation from one who does not understand her role. Keep the discussion private if that helps her speak freely.

sections.title: Choose an action she can control
paragraphs: Replace a broad demand with a small football action. A midfielder might try moving into a passing lane after giving the ball away. A winger might attempt one change of pace when space opens outside. Agree the action with the player rather than announcing a target for her. It should be challenging enough to mean something and manageable enough to try. Success begins with recognising the opportunity and making an attempt; the defender may still win the ball.

sections.title: Build the challenge gradually
paragraphs: A coach can start with a predictable pass, add a defender who applies light pressure, then move into a small game. The player needs time at each stage to work out what helps. Repeating the easiest version forever will not prepare her for opposition, but moving straight to a crowded game can hide the skill you want her to learn. Adjust space, speed or numbers one at a time. Ask what changed when the task became harder.

sections.title: Give feedback that explains progress
paragraphs: Useful encouragement names something real: she looked before receiving, tried the turn at a better moment, or offered for the ball again after a mistake. Avoid praising every action identically or promising that she will beat the defender next time. Players can recognise when praise does not match the game. Notice thoughtful decisions as well as successful outcomes. A good choice can fail because the pass was slightly inaccurate or an opponent reacted well.

sections.title: Keep difficult days in perspective
paragraphs: After a hard match, allow the player to decide when she wants to talk. One performance is a small part of her football experience. If a worry keeps returning, speak with the coach about the situations they see and what support is possible. If the issue is repeated humiliation, exclusion or bullying, take the concern seriously instead of treating it as a confidence exercise. Feeling safe and being treated respectfully come before persuading someone to be braver.

practice: For the next session, let her choose one “I will try” action. Afterwards ask whether she noticed an opportunity, what she tried and what might make the next attempt easier. Do not count every mistake or compare her with a teammate. Keep a short note in her own words so she can recognise changes over several weeks.
takeaways: Identify a specific situation before choosing a target.
Notice attempts and decisions as well as outcomes.
Let the player help decide the next step.

title: Home practice that fits around real life
summary: Create short, purposeful ball sessions with simple equipment and room for choice.
intro: Home practice works best when a player understands what she is exploring and wants to have a go. It does not need a garden full of equipment or a parent acting as a second coach. A ball, a suitable space and one clear idea can be enough. The aim is to connect a small practice task to something she recognises in football, while leaving room for school, friends and time away from the game.

sections.title: Start with a useful question
paragraphs: Ask what she would like to feel more comfortable doing. Perhaps the ball gets caught under her feet when she turns, or her first touch takes her towards an opponent. Choose one problem rather than a list of weaknesses. If her coach has assigned a practice, use that as the starting point and ask for a demonstration if needed. Avoid adding several extra programmes simply because they look impressive online. More tasks can make the purpose harder to remember.

sections.title: Make the space suitable
paragraphs: Check the surface, nearby windows, people, pets and objects before starting. Use a ball appropriate to the space and get permission before using a wall. Do not practise near roads or use furniture as jumping equipment. A narrow indoor area might suit gentle sole touches or rolling the ball across the body; it may be unsuitable for shooting or quick changes of direction. Change the activity to fit the space instead of forcing the full drill into it.

sections.title: Use a simple three-part session
paragraphs: For an optional ten-minute example, spend a couple of minutes moving gently with the ball, several minutes exploring one skill, then finish with a small challenge the player chooses. She might receive a gentle pass and take her first touch through either of two gates. Keep the gates wide at first. A younger beginner may prefer an imaginative game with a family member. A more experienced player may want to test different receiving angles. The example is a flexible starting point, not a daily requirement.

sections.title: Add a decision, not just more speed
paragraphs: Once the movement is comfortable, introduce a small piece of information. A partner can stand near one gate, leaving the other available, or roll a pass from a slightly different angle. The player then has a reason to adjust her touch. Keep enough time for her to look and decide. If every attempt becomes rushed, remove some pressure. A solo practice is useful for ball familiarity, but it cannot reproduce all the choices created by teammates and opponents.

sections.title: Finish while the purpose is still clear
paragraphs: Ask which version felt useful and what she might try in her next session. You do not need a leaderboard, video of every attempt or a record of every touch. If she is tired, sore or simply needs a break, stop and discuss a different time or task. Home practice should support her football rather than become a punishment for a poor match. A coach can help adapt an activity if it repeatedly feels uncomfortable or confusing.

practice: Set two wide gates with safe markers. Receive a gentle pass, look at the available gate and guide the first touch towards it. Begin without a defender. Then let a partner move towards one gate before the ball arrives. Swap roles so both people experience choosing and supplying the pass. Finish by naming where the same decision could appear in a match.
takeaways: Choose one purpose and a suitable space.
Add information and choice when the basic task is comfortable.
Treat extra practice as optional support, not a punishment.

title: Scanning: know what is around you before the ball arrives
summary: Turn looking over a shoulder into information that helps the next decision.
intro: A player can move her head repeatedly and still be unsure what to do when the ball arrives. Scanning is useful when it answers a football question: where is the nearest opponent, where is there space, and which teammate might be available? The point is to collect information she can use. The following examples are STAR practice suggestions; the linked FA guides offer further explanation of scanning and receiving.

sections.title: Look for something specific
paragraphs: Start with one question rather than asking a player to see everything. A central midfielder might check whether pressure is coming from her left or right. A wide player might check the space along the touchline before receiving. Ask her what she noticed, without turning the conversation into a memory test. If she cannot identify anything useful, simplify the situation. The aim is to connect a glance with an action, not reward head movement for its own sake.

sections.title: Choose moments when a glance is possible
paragraphs: Looking away while trying to control an awkward pass can make the task harder. Explore moments before the pass is played or while the ball is travelling predictably. The player still needs to return her attention to the ball. Information also changes: a defender who was far away may accelerate as the pass leaves a teammate’s foot. Treat the first look as a starting picture and check it again when the situation allows, rather than assuming the space will remain open.

sections.title: Let body position help the picture
paragraphs: A player who stands square to the passer may find it difficult to see behind her. A slight adjustment of position can bring more of the pitch into view. There is no single stance that suits every pass. If a defender is close, protecting the ball or returning it may be the sensible option. Help the player explore which position lets her see the ball and the relevant space without losing balance or exposing possession unnecessarily.

sections.title: Use an opponent to make information matter
paragraphs: In an original starter activity, place two receiving gates behind a player and ask a partner to occupy one before a gentle pass arrives. She checks which gate is open and takes her touch that way. Give her time to succeed before adding movement or reducing space. Then try a small game where she must choose between turning, carrying and returning the pass. A colour call can introduce looking, but an opponent’s position has a clearer connection to a football decision.

sections.title: Review the choice, not just the result
paragraphs: After a moment in practice, ask what she saw and whether it influenced her first touch. If she turned into pressure, consider whether she looked too early, missed the opponent or struggled to execute the touch. These are different problems. Do not stop every passage of play to question her. Choose occasional moments and allow uninterrupted attempts. Look for the habit appearing naturally in different parts of the pitch, including when the best decision is a simple pass backwards.

practice: Watch one receiving moment together. Pause before the pass arrives and name the nearest pressure, the clearest space and one support option. Play the clip and compare those options with the player’s decision. There may be several reasonable answers. Return to a live ball activity so the discussion stays connected to playing.
takeaways: Give each glance a football question.
Information can change while the ball travels.
Returning the ball can be a good decision.

sources.label: The FA: How to help players improve their receiving skills

title: A first touch with a purpose
summary: Practise receiving for the action that comes next, rather than stopping every pass.
intro: A good first touch is not always a perfectly still ball. Sometimes the useful touch moves into space; sometimes it keeps the ball close, cushions an awkward pass or prepares a return pass. What makes it useful is the situation that follows. A player who can stop ten identical passes still needs opportunities to adjust when the angle, speed and pressure change. Begin with control, then connect that control to a choice.

sections.title: Decide what the touch needs to achieve
paragraphs: Before a practice begins, identify the next action. Is the player preparing to pass, turn away from pressure or carry into a gap? This gives the task a purpose. Avoid demanding that every pass must be received on one particular foot regardless of the situation. A touch across the body can help when there is space on the far side, but the same touch can expose the ball if a defender is waiting there. Let the player explain the space she wants to use.

sections.title: Make the pass part of the practice
paragraphs: Receiving depends partly on what arrives. Start with a partner who can deliver a manageable pass, then gradually vary its pace and direction. The receiver can move to improve the angle rather than remain fixed behind a cone. If the supply is repeatedly too difficult, adjust the distance or speed so there are meaningful attempts. When both players swap roles, discuss how the passer can help: timing, accuracy and the weight of the ball all influence the receiver’s options.

sections.title: Explore different contact and distances
paragraphs: The inside of the foot may help cushion a pass or move it across the body. The outside can sometimes take the ball away from an approaching opponent. The sole may be useful for a controlled stop or change of direction. These are options to explore with a coach rather than a checklist to use on every pass. Ask how far the ball needs to travel. A larger touch may suit open space, while a closer touch may help when pressure is near.

sections.title: Move from gates into a game
paragraphs: Use a receiving area with two exits. Begin with the player choosing an exit before the pass, then allow a defender to block one route. Finally add a supporting teammate, so returning the pass becomes an option too. Keep the area generous enough for the player to recognise the picture. Changing one constraint at a time helps reveal whether difficulty comes from control, awareness or a rushed decision. Avoid treating the gate exercise as the finished skill.

sections.title: Understand why an attempt broke down
paragraphs: If the ball escapes, ask whether the player had to stretch, met the pass with a stiff foot or chose space that was already closing. A slower demonstration can clarify the movement. Then return to realistic pace when she is ready. Do not make her replay a mistake until she feels embarrassed. A short adjustment followed by several fresh attempts is usually a more useful coaching conversation. Notice when her touch creates time even if the following pass is imperfect.

practice: With a partner, practise receiving towards a safe exit and making a short pass back. Change the passing angle after a few attempts. Let the receiver choose when to keep the ball close and when to move it further. Add a light, predictable defender only when both players understand the task, and let the receiver return the ball if both exits close.
takeaways: Judge the touch by the next action it allows.
Vary the pass as well as the receiving movement.
Keep awareness, control and choice connected.

title: Beating a defender: timing, space and a change of pace
summary: Make one-to-one attacking about reading the opponent, not memorising tricks.
intro: A turn or step-over can look impressive without moving an opponent. In a match, the attacker needs to recognise where the defender is, which space is available and when to accelerate. A simple change of direction can be enough if the timing is right. Give a player several ways to solve a one-to-one situation, including combining with a teammate. Beating someone is an option, not a requirement every time she receives.

sections.title: Know where you want to go
paragraphs: Give the attacker a destination that resembles a football problem: two gates, a scoring zone or space to cross. Without a destination, she may perform a move without gaining an advantage. Ask which route looks available as she approaches. The touchline can limit one side, while a recovering opponent can close another. Begin with a clear picture and enough room to explore. The attacker should understand what she is trying to achieve before the defender begins applying pressure.

sections.title: Approach with the ball available
paragraphs: A player needs touches that allow her to change direction rather than chase the ball. She can experiment with a slower approach, a pause or a slight angle towards the defender. Avoid one fixed instruction about the exact distance at which every move must happen. Speed, space and the defender’s reach change the problem. If the defender wins possession before the player can act, make the starting distance greater and explore what she notices on the approach.

sections.title: Make the opponent respond
paragraphs: A movement of the body, a change of running line or a suggestion of a pass can draw a response. The useful question is whether the defender shifts, slows or leaves a route available. The attacker then needs a touch into that space and a change of pace. Rehearsing the movement without opposition can build familiarity, but a live defender helps her discover when it works. Encourage her to watch what happens instead of completing the whole sequence automatically.

sections.title: Practise both outcomes
paragraphs: Sometimes the defender stays balanced and the gap does not appear. Let the attacker protect possession, change the question or use a support player. A practice that only rewards dribbling past an opponent can teach her to ignore a better pass. Rotate roles so she also experiences what makes an attacker difficult to defend. Keep challenges controlled and appropriate to the players. Stop unsafe contact and avoid celebrating physical intimidation as an attacking skill.

sections.title: Connect the move to the next action
paragraphs: Getting past the first defender does not finish the attack. Add a target pass, a controlled finish or a decision about when to release the ball. If the touch after the move is too large, an opponent may recover. If it is too small, the attacker may lose the space she created. Discuss what the next picture requires. In a match review, notice a well-timed attempt even when a second defender prevents the final action.

practice: Set two wide gates and allow the attacker to score by carrying through either. Give the defender a controlled starting position and swap roles frequently. Later add a teammate behind the attacker as a safe passing option. Discuss when the attacker noticed a clear route, when the defender recovered and when keeping possession was the better choice.
takeaways: Give the attacker a destination and a real choice.
Watch the defender’s response before choosing the exit.
Practise the action after getting past.

sources.label: England Football Learning: The FA 4 Corner Model

title: Useful movement when you do not have the ball
summary: Help teammates by changing passing angles, creating space and moving at the right moment.
intro: Players can contribute to an attack without touching the ball. A small move can open a passing lane, take a defender away or give the ball carrier a safe way out. That contribution is easy to miss if we only count goals and assists. Start with the relationship between two players: where is the ball, what can the teammate see and what movement might help her next decision?

sections.title: Become visible to the passer
paragraphs: If an opponent stands directly between you and the ball, calling louder may not create a pass. A short move to either side can change the angle. Check that the passer can realistically deliver the ball before making a long run. A teammate under pressure may need a close option rather than someone sprinting away. Encourage the receiver to notice the ball carrier’s body position as well as her own marker. Useful support responds to the person with possession.

sections.title: Use distance deliberately
paragraphs: Standing close can help a short combination, but several teammates crowding the ball can remove space. Standing further away may stretch an opponent, yet make the pass difficult for a younger player. There is no universal correct distance. Explore what the passer can achieve and where the next defender is. In a small game, pause occasionally to compare a crowded picture with one in which players offer different angles. Let the players feel how the options change.

sections.title: Time the movement
paragraphs: Arriving early in a space can allow a defender to follow and close it. Arriving as the passer becomes ready may create a clearer opportunity. A receiver can first move away, then change direction towards the ball, or delay a run until a teammate looks up. These are possibilities rather than compulsory patterns. The aim is to coordinate movement with the pass. A well-timed short movement can be more helpful than constant running with no connection to play.

sections.title: Recognise runs that help someone else
paragraphs: A wide run may pull a defender towards the touchline and create a gap for another player. A forward can move away from the ball and give a midfielder room to carry. The pass does not have to arrive for the movement to matter. Ask players what changed around the runner. Avoid praising every decoy run automatically: if nobody reacts and the ball carrier loses a support option, a different movement might have helped more.

sections.title: Keep learning through small games
paragraphs: A three-against-two possession game can make support angles easier to notice. Allow players to move freely rather than holding them on cones throughout. If the defenders win every ball immediately, enlarge the space or adjust the challenge. If possession is effortless, add a directional target. Ask one question between rounds, such as where the passer needed help. Then let the game continue. Endless instructions from the side can prevent the players from communicating with each other.

practice: Watch a short passage of play and follow one player who does not receive the ball. Notice when she changes angle, moves a defender or offers support behind possession. In the next practice, choose one of those ideas to explore. Do not judge the entire activity by how many passes she receives; look at whether her movement makes a useful option available.
takeaways: Move to change the picture for a teammate.
Different angles are often more helpful than crowding the ball.
A run can matter even when the pass goes elsewhere.

title: Defending with patience and purpose
summary: Explore positioning, delaying and choosing a moment to challenge.
intro: Good defending is not measured only by tackles. A player may help her team by slowing an attack, protecting a route towards goal or allowing a teammate to recover. Charging towards every opponent can make her easy to beat. Begin with the problem she is solving: what needs protecting, where is support, and what can she influence safely? Contact practice should be supervised by a coach who can adapt it to the players.

sections.title: Protect something that matters
paragraphs: Give the defender a clear target to protect, such as a gate or scoring zone. This helps her understand why she needs a particular position. If she only chases the attacker, the route to the target may remain open. Ask where she can stand to make the most dangerous route harder to use. The answer changes with the ball’s location and the help behind her. Avoid teaching a fixed stance without explaining the purpose of the position.

sections.title: Approach without losing control
paragraphs: A defender may need to travel quickly while the ball is far away, then adjust her steps as she gets closer. Arriving too fast can leave her unable to respond to a change of direction. Practise closing space against an attacker who initially moves at a manageable pace. Let the defender discover a distance from which she can influence the ball without reaching and losing balance. Increase the challenge gradually rather than demanding a tackle on every attempt.

sections.title: Delay can be a successful outcome
paragraphs: If the attacker has support and the defender is temporarily alone, keeping the attack in front of her may be valuable. A few controlled moments can allow teammates to recover. This does not mean backing away indefinitely or refusing to challenge. It means recognising that winning the ball immediately is not always realistic. Give the practice an outcome that rewards protecting the target for a short period as well as regaining possession, so the player experiences both choices.

sections.title: Notice a possible moment to challenge
paragraphs: A touch that moves the ball away from the attacker may create an opportunity. So may a pass that arrives slowly enough to intercept. The defender still needs to consider her distance and the consequences of missing. A coach can demonstrate how to approach these situations safely and within the rules of the player’s competition. Do not encourage lunging, pushing or deliberately frightening an opponent. Courage includes making a controlled decision when the game feels fast.

sections.title: Connect with teammates and the next action
paragraphs: When another defender is nearby, communication can clarify who engages the ball and who protects the space behind. Keep the language simple and agreed within the team. After regaining possession, the player needs to look for a safe next action rather than assume the work is finished. If she is beaten, encourage recovery towards a useful position. Criticism shouted during the chase rarely tells her where help is needed. Review the picture at a calmer moment.

practice: In a coach-led activity, use a wide gate and controlled one-against-one approaches. Begin without tackling: the defender scores by delaying the attacker’s route, while the attacker scores by carrying through the gate. Later introduce appropriately supervised opportunities to win possession. Swap roles and discuss which approaches made the attacker change direction or slow down.
takeaways: Protect the route as well as responding to the ball.
A controlled delay can help the team recover.
Practise a useful action after winning possession.

sources.label: England Football Learning: The FA 4 Corner Model

title: Turn coaching feedback into something you can try
summary: Ask clearer questions, practise one adjustment and review what changes.
intro: “Open up”, “be stronger” and “play quicker” may mean something specific to a coach but remain unclear to a player. Useful feedback gives her an action she can recognise and attempt. She does not need to understand everything immediately or treat correction as a judgement on her ability. The aim is a conversation that connects what happened, what might help and when she can try it again.

sections.title: Ask for the football example
paragraphs: If a phrase is unclear, ask the coach to show the situation. Where was the defender? Which way could the receiver see? What did the next pass need? A demonstration or a quick walk-through may help more than repeating the instruction louder. Players can ask whether the advice applies every time or only in that picture. This is especially useful when a phrase sounds absolute, such as “always turn”, but the match contains situations where turning would lose possession.

sections.title: Choose one adjustment
paragraphs: A player may receive several observations after a session. Agree which one matters most for the next attempt. If she is learning to receive away from pressure, the immediate focus could be checking the opponent’s side before the pass arrives. Trying to change her stance, touch, passing speed and movement all at once can make the task confusing. Keep the whole football problem in view, but give her one clear starting point she can remember.

sections.title: Try the suggestion in a suitable task
paragraphs: Ask for an opportunity to practise the adjustment at a manageable level, then use it against realistic opposition. A player may understand the explanation yet need time to coordinate the movement. If the task is too fast, slow it down briefly or increase the space. If it is too predictable, add a decision. The important question is whether she can recognise when the advice applies, rather than simply repeat the movement in isolation.

sections.title: Tell the coach what happened
paragraphs: After an attempt, describe something concrete: the touch created more space, the defender followed, or the movement felt difficult when the pass came faster. That helps the coach decide what to change. A player does not need to agree that an instruction helped if it still feels unclear. Equally, one unsuccessful attempt does not prove the idea is useless. Look at several attempts and consider the pass, the opposition and the timing before deciding what to work on next.

sections.title: Handle different coaching messages calmly
paragraphs: A club coach may ask a player to hold width while an individual coach explores moving inside. These can both make sense in different situations. Ask about the purpose and respect the club’s team instructions during its matches. Avoid placing the player between adults or asking her to prove that one coach is right. If advice remains contradictory, adults can discuss the examples constructively. At home, ask what she understood and wants to try; leave room for a conversation about something other than football.

practice: Use a short feedback note with three lines: “The situation was…”, “I will try…” and “I will notice whether…”. For example, receiving near the touchline, checking inside before the pass and noticing whether a return pass or turn is available. Bring the example back to the coach and ask for a review after the next session.
takeaways: Ask for a demonstration when words are unclear.
Practise one adjustment and recognise when it applies.
Explain what changed so feedback becomes a conversation.
